performance.","Preference driven by the desire to maximize the informational value of the next trial."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a pilot prefers a plane model with a long safety record not because it guarantees no crashes, but because it has survived diverse conditions, scientists prefer corroborated theories to subject them to new, diverse conditions.","The rationality of the choice lies in the structure of the testing regime, not in the statistical likelihood of the outcome."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a non-inductive methodological rule akin to a gambler preferring a die that has not yet shown bias: the preference is rational because it maximizes the severity of potential falsification in the next test, not because it increases the probability of success.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper admits that acting on a theory implies an expectation of its practical success (e.g., the bridge won't fall), then the distinction between corroboration and probability collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'Severity Maximization' argument cannot explain why a scientist would personally rely on the theory for life-critical decisions rather than just proposing it for further testing.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the analogy of the 'gambler' secretly relies on the uniformity of nature (that the die will behave tomorrow as it did today), which is the very inductive principle Popper rejects.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Severity Maximization': choosing the best-corroborated theory is the only choice that keeps the game of science going by subjecting the most resilient survivor to the hardest possible next test. If we chose a poorly tested theory, we would risk a trivial falsification or miss the chance to learn from a deep error. Thus, the 'practical' act of building a bridge on a corroborated theory is not a belief in its safety (induction), but a commitment to test the limits of our current knowledge under load; if it fails, we learn more than if we built it on a weak theory.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
